title: Response pathway cohort breakdown & per-stage attribution
content:
Summary:
This working note records an experiment set and trace analysis that breaks end-to-end response time into per-stage contributions across tagged cohorts. Goal: find the dominant sources of p95/p99 skew we see in production for gen-chat and reduce tail by 30–50% via targeted mitigations (async batching, KV-cache priming, network path optimizations).

Why this doc: We have many short investigations (sampling, waterfall analyses) but lacked a compact cohort-driven view that ties p50/p95/p99 to stage-by-stage timings across realistic request labels. This doc captures method, sample data, and prioritized remediation plan.

Instrumentation and sampling method:
- Trace collection window: 2024-09-10 00:00 UTC through 2024-09-14 23:59 UTC
- Sampling: 1 in 50 requests captured at the edge, with additional targeted sampling for long-tail requests (latency > 1s) after 2024-09-12 to enrich p99.
- Span model: ingress -> auth -> routing -> deserialize -> tokenize -> model-exec (split: kv-lookup, attention-kernel, matmul-kernel, kv-write) -> postprocess -> egress
- Cohorts (tagged at router):
  * cohort:short-gen (expected output tokens < 32)
  * cohort:long-gen (expected output tokens > 128)
  * cohort:cold-kv (first request for user -> kv-cache miss)
  * cohort:warm-kv (user has recent KV prefix cached)
  * cohort:high-concurrency (client QPS spikes > 40/s per session)
- Hardware baseline for traces: G5-like instance (48GB GPU), 8 vCPU model worker, 100GbE egress path.

Aggregate p50/p95/p99 by cohort (ms):
-------------------------------------------------------------
cohort           | p50   | p95   | p99   | sample_count
-------------------------------------------------------------
short-gen        | 85    | 210   | 490   | 9,420
long-gen         | 420   | 1,150 | 2,300 | 3,120
cold-kv          | 150   | 620   | 1,700 | 2,700
warm-kv          | 78    | 180   | 420   | 8,010
high-concurrency | 240   | 920   | 1,900 | 1,800
-------------------------------------------------------------
Notes: short-gen p95 dominated by network stalls and batching wait; long-gen naturally heavier on model-exec but tail shows kernel contention and occasional mem-swap events.

Per-stage median and tail attribution (example cohort: short-gen):
- ingress: p50=6ms, p95=12ms, p99=18ms (network edge -> router; stable)
- auth: p50=1ms, p95=3ms, p99=6ms (negligible)
- routing: p50=5ms, p95=30ms, p99=120ms (high variance when fallback routing triggers cross-region)
- deserialize: p50=2ms, p95=4ms, p99=8ms
- tokenize: p50=4ms, p95=10ms, p99=28ms
- model-exec(total): p50=55ms, p95=140ms, p99=380ms  
    * kv-lookup: p50=6ms, p95=40ms, p99=160ms  
    * attention/kernel: p50=32ms, p95=80ms, p99=180ms
    * matmul kernels & small ops: p50=12ms, p95=20ms, p99=40ms
    * kv-write: p50=2ms, p95=10ms, p99=30ms
- postprocess: p50=2ms, p95=8ms, p99=20ms
- egress: p50=3ms, p95=18ms, p99=40ms

Attribution percentages (short-gen p99 = 490ms):
- model-exec: 66% (≈325ms)
- batching wait + routing delays: 16% (≈80ms)
- network/ingress/egress: 6% (≈30ms)
- tokenize+deserialize+postprocess: 6% (≈30ms)
- auth & misc: 6% (≈25ms)

Key observations and hypotheses:
1) Routing fallbacks (cross-region or model-variant fallback) are overrepresented in p99 for short-gen and warm-kv cohorts. We observed a handful of traces where routing added 300–800ms due to cross-region hop. Hypothesis: routing policy timeouts and health-check flapping cause synchronous fallback.
2) KV-cache cold misses explain large fraction of cold-kv p95/p99 spikes. KV-lookup on miss triggers extra model exec work (prefix re-encode) and occasionally forces a cold load of user-specific embeddings from slow NVMe.
3) High concurrency spikes cause queuing on the GPU worker side and periodic kernel contention that increases attention/kernel p99 by 2–3x.
4) There are ~12 traces where post-kernel page faults correlated with host memory pressure; these line up with long-gen p99 events.
5) Batching wait is a large contributor for short-gen p95: many clients are single-request synchronous patterns which drift in time; default batch wait of 10ms trades off throughput but inflates p95.

Representative trace vignettes (anonymized trace ids):
- TRACE-A-14421 (short-gen, p99=512ms): routing fallback (230ms) + model-exec attention stall (160ms) + kv-lookup heat (80ms)
- TRACE-B-6609 (long-gen, p99=2,340ms): kernel queuing under high concurrency + swap-related stall (∼700ms)
- TRACE-C-2810 (cold-kv, p95=720ms): nvme read for user embeddings (420ms) + extra tokenization step (50ms) + batching wait (70ms)

Experiment matrix run (short summaries):
- Experiment 1: routing soft-timeout reduced from 250ms->80ms for canary region (impact: reduced routing p99 contribution from median 120ms->30ms for affected subset). JIRA: JIRA-SRV-4038.
- Experiment 2: KV-prefetch for active sessions (prefetch top-3 prefixes): reduced cold-kv p95 by ~28% on sample. Note: increased read amplification; further cost analysis needed.
- Experiment 3: dynamic batch wait policy (adaptive wait based on per-route instantaneous QPS): p95 for short-gen reduced 18% in canary with negligible throughput loss.
- Experiment 4: host memory cap enforcement + earlier eviction for long-running sessions: removed the page-fault correlated p99 tail in 3/4 reproductions.

Shortlist of mitigations (prioritized):
1) Make routing fallback asynchronous where possible; fail-fast with local fallback rather than cross-region synchronous hop. Owner: Diego. (High impact, medium effort)
2) Implement KV-prefetch for sessions with repeated prefixes + eviction policy to limit NVMe reads. Owner: Priya. (High impact, experimental)
3) Ship adaptive batch-wait with route-level SLO tuning and a short-circuit for short-gen paths. Owner: Maya. (Medium impact, low effort)
4) Add host-side memory headroom metrics to the scheduler and enforce preemptive eviction to avoid page-fault stalls. Owner: Evan. (Medium impact, medium effort)
5) Kernel-level telemetry: increase sampling for matmul/attention kernels to capture contention windows; tie to scheduler decisions. Owner: infra-kernel-team. (Low impact initially, enables future tuning)

Action items (next 6 weeks):
- Week 1: rollout routing soft-timeout canary + observability dashboards (Diego).
- Week 2: deploy adaptive batch-wait canary on 5% of traffic for short-gen routes (Maya + DevEx).
- Week 3–4: KV-prefetch small-scale experiment for top-10 customers contributing to cold-kv cohort (Priya).
- Week 4–6: kernel telemetry increase and memory-eviction policy pilots (Evan + infra).

Open questions / risks:
- Cost of KV-prefetch at scale: needs chargeback model and SLO boundaries.
- Some routing health checks may mask root cause (upstream infra flapping); need to correlate with SRE alerts before attributing to routing logic.
- Adaptive batching may shift tail into downstream systems (e.g., egress); end-to-end monitoring must be in place.

Appendix: quick reproducible checklist for trace collection
- enable trace-sampling config: trace.sample_rate=1/50
- turn on enriched kv telemetry: mv_kv.enriched=true (for experiment window only)
- snapshot gpu kernel logs via /debug/kernel-sampled every 30s
- mark canary routes with header X-rt-cohort=short-gen-canary

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working doc: numbers are sample-derived and may change with more data. Please add trace ids you find suspicious to the "linked_artifacts" list and annotate with findings.
- If you want the raw trace bundle (.ndjson) for the collection window, ping me and I will share a secure link.

End of note.
